Naples ’44
About Timeline Places People Folklore Themes

Theme

Superstition & religion

Miracles, saints, folk magic, the evil eye, ritual

Appears in 9 diary entries.

  1. October 8 1943
    Floods of dubious civilian tips overwhelm the section, including a "spy" who turns out to be rumored a witch by superstitious villagers.
    • Superstition & religion
    • Bureaucracy & absurdity
  2. March 22 1944
    Lewis travels through falling ash and volcanic debris to report on the threatened town of San Sebastiano as lava approaches.
    • Superstition & religion
  3. March 24 1944
    With the eruption subsiding, Lewis meets Del Giudice, an eccentric folklore writer and expert on San Gennaro and Vesuvius.
    • Superstition & religion
  4. March 25 1944
    Widespread fear that San Gennaro's blood may fail to liquefy reflects a surge of religious "miracle" fervor sweeping wartime Naples.
    • Superstition & religion
  5. March 29 1944
    More reported miracles sweep the region, including a visionary child and a monk claimed to have flown to rescue a downed pilot.
    • Superstition & religion
  6. May 7 (i) 1944
    San Gennaro's blood liquefies, but slowly — considered a bad omen — after days of anxious public vigil that could have sparked unrest if it had failed.
    • Superstition & religion
  7. June 27 1944
    A colleague describes a revived, medieval-style flagellant procession at Guardia Sanframondi; two more feast stories follow — Nola's Feast of the Lily disrupting army telephone lines, and a trip to Amalfi for the thrice-yearly 'manna' relic of St Andrew.
    • Superstition & religion
  8. September 3 1944
    Following Don Ubaldo's death, the section relocates to a remote, archaic hill village with its own strange local fox-cult ritual.
    • Superstition & religion
  9. September 23 1944
    Lewis realizes with unease that locals now regard him as a possible *jettatore* (bearer of the evil eye), noting superstitious gestures made in his presence. He then reflects that a year after liberation, still hungry and diseased amid lawless ruins with only the distant promise of corrupt democracy ahead, Neapolitans may reasonably look back on the Mussolini years as a lost paradise by comparison.
    • Superstition & religion
    • Personal reflection
